newsitem.title: USA: Cohen outlines U.S. defense plan to top lawmakers.
newsitem.headline: Cohen outlines U.S. defense plan to top lawmakers.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen on Thursday presented to congressional leaders a new plan for U.S. military strategy, force cuts and arms modernisation into the next century.

Cohen was silent at a photo session, but defence officials have said the quadrennial defence review, due to be made public on Monday, called for new base closings and shrinking costly jet fighter programmes. But it would cut only some 60,000 troops from the 1.4 million-member military.
The controversial "QDR" is designed to match superpower strategy with force levels and arms modernisation into the 21st century.

Bright flowers centred each of three tables in Cohen's office where he fed breakfast and charts full of figures to about 30 senior lawmakers and staffers from four key security and appropriations committees of the House and Senate.

Cohen also was outlining the controversial plan, which has already drawn criticism from members of Congress and defence analysts as not sweeping enough, at a Pentagon lunch for former Defence Secretaries William Perry, Harold Brown, Dick Cheney, Elliot Richardson and Donald Rumsfeld.
Lawmakers do not want to close more bases, which are a financial boon to many communities in the nation, and many analysts say that the QDR changes are not sweeping enough.

Cohen, who retired earlier this year as a Republican senator from Maine, was flanked at his breakfast table by Chairmen Floyd Spense, a South Carolina Republican, of the House National Security Committee and Ted Stevens, an Alaska Republican, of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
Senior Republican and Democratic lawmakers and staff directors from the Senate Armed Services Committee and House Appropriations Committees also attended.

Cohen has described the QDR results as a compromise to face the realities of growing demands on the military such as fighting wars, keeping the peace and performing humanitarian duties along with saving save money to spend on needed arms modernisation for the 21st century.

Some defence analysts have said more sweeping changes are needed, such as completely realigning Army divisions. And some have said the expectation of $250 billion defence budgets for the long term is unrealistic because of future demands from other federal programmes.

Cohen emphasised in recent weeks that the death of the Soviet Union had not ended international threats to U.S. security and that more domestic military bases must be shut to save money for new high-tech weapons.

He made clear that the United States would retain its current strategy of being prepared to fight two major regional conflicts at once and will keep 100,000 troops in Europe and another 100,000 in the western Pacific.

Defence officials earlier confirmed a Washington Post report that Cohen planned to seek a cut of about 60,000 active duty military personnel, 70,000 military reservists and some 80,000 civilian Defence Department personnel.

They said Cohen had decided to reduce by more than 300 -- but not cancel -- the planned purchase of Air Force F-22 and Navy FA-18E/F fighter jets in programmes under development by Lockheed Martin Corp. and McDonnell Douglas Corp.
Cohen was expected to recommend that the Air Force's previously planned purchase of 438 F-22s be reduced to 339. The cost of that programme under the full buy had been estimated at about $67 billion.

He was also expected to recommend that Navy purchases of the advanced FA-18E/F be cut to about 785 or perhaps fewer from 1,000. The Navy had planned to buy 1,000 of the aircraft for about $80 bilion by 2015.
